title: The Drowned Nations: Pacific Islander Heritage in the GLMZ

# The Drowned Nations: Pacific Islander Heritage in the GLMZ

## Nations That No Longer Exist

Tuvalu was the first sovereign nation to be formally dissolved due to sea level rise. On March 14, 2067, the Tuvaluan government-in-exile — operating from a rented office building in Suva, Fiji — signed the Final Instrument of Dissolution, acknowledging that no habitable land remained within its territorial boundaries. Funafuti atoll had been permanently submerged since 2059. The last residents had been evacuated in 2054. Tuvalu's total population at dissolution was 14,200 people scattered across seventeen host nations, carrying passports from a country that existed only as a coordinate on nautical charts.

Kiribati followed in 2071. The Marshall Islands in 2074. Nauru — already devastated by a century of phosphate mining — went under in 2069, though by then fewer than 800 people still claimed Nauruan citizenship. The Federated States of Micronesia lost its last inhabited island in 2078. Palau held on until 2083, its Rock Islands reduced to a navigational hazard for automated shipping lanes.

The larger Pacific Island nations survived in diminished form. Samoa lost its coastal population centers but retained high-elevation settlements. Tonga's Tongatapu — home to 70% of the national population — was permanently flooded by 2075, but the volcanic islands of Ha'apai and Vava'u remained above water. Fiji lost Suva and most of Viti Levu's coastal lowlands but retained functional sovereignty through its highland interior. Papua New Guinea's sheer geographic mass preserved it, though its coastal populations were displaced inland at a scale that destabilized the nation for decades.

The total pre-displacement population of the Pacific Islands was approximately 12 million people. By 2090, an estimated 9.8 million had been permanently displaced from their homelands. The displacement rate — roughly 82% — was the highest of any regional population on Earth. For the smallest atoll nations, displacement was 100%. Every citizen. Every family. Every generation from that point forward would live somewhere their ancestors had never been.

## The Path to the Great Lakes

Pacific Islanders did not arrive in the GLMZ in a single wave. The migration unfolded across three generations, each driven by different pressures.

The first wave, 2050s through 2070s, was the emergency evacuation phase. International resettlement programs placed Pacific Island refugees primarily in Australia, New Zealand, and the American West Coast. But Australia's own climate crisis — the desertification of the Murray-Darling Basin, the abandonment of Adelaide — limited its absorption capacity. New Zealand, with a population under 6 million, could not absorb millions. The West Coast of the United States was simultaneously dealing with the Pacific Northwest wildfire evacuations and the cascading infrastructure failures of the California water crisis.

The second wave, 2080s through 2110s, brought Pacific Islanders from these initial host regions to the Great Lakes as secondary displacement took hold. When the West Coast collapsed, everyone on it moved — including the Pacific Islander communities that had settled in Portland, Seattle, and Sacramento less than a generation earlier. The phrase "twice displaced" entered the Pacific Islander lexicon during this period, carrying a weight that non-Islander populations struggled to comprehend. To lose your homeland to the ocean was devastating. To lose your new home to wildfire and drought within a single lifetime was something else entirely.

The third wave, 2120s through 2160s, was economic migration. By this point, the GLMZ was the dominant economic engine of the North American continent, and Pacific Islander communities already established there served as anchor populations. Mass driver routes connecting Pacific Rim transit hubs to the GLMZ corridor made the journey trivial — a four-hour ride from the Auckland terminal to the Lambeau Terminus.

## The Memory Keepers

Pacific Islander communities in the GLMZ maintain the most active homeland memory culture of any diaspora group in the megacity. This is not nostalgia. This is the preservation of nations that no longer physically exist.

The Vaka Moana Cultural Conservancy, headquartered in the Gray Zone's Level 12 communal halls, maintains digital reconstructions of every submerged atoll nation — topographic maps, architectural records, oral histories, navigational star charts, and genealogical databases stretching back forty generations. The Conservancy's position is explicit: these nations were not abandoned. They were taken. The ocean took them. The carbon that raised the ocean was not Pacific Islander carbon.

Language preservation is fierce. Tuvaluan, Marshallese, Gilbertese, Nauruan — languages that once had fewer than 20,000 speakers each — are taught in community schools funded by collective Φ contributions. The GLMZ's Tuvaluan-speaking population in 2226 is estimated at 8,400 — larger than the population of Tuvalu at any point in the 20th century. The language lives because the people decided it would.

## District Concentration and Daily Life

Pacific Islanders concentrate in the Gray Zone and The Underworld, with smaller communities in Old Harbor. the Gray Zone's communal housing structures suit a culture built on extended family networks — the Samoan aiga, the Tongan kainga. Multi-generational households of fifteen to twenty people occupying connected units are common, and Pacific Islander families have a reputation for converting standard the Gray Zone housing into something warmer and louder than the architects intended.

The Underworld presence dates to the early compression era, when newly arrived Pacific Islander workers took infrastructure maintenance jobs in the sub-grade levels — water treatment, tunnel repair, power routing. The work was hard, dangerous, and poorly paid, but it was steady, and it was familiar to people who had spent their lives maintaining infrastructure against the ocean. Two centuries later, Pacific Islander families still dominate several Underworld maintenance guilds, and the sub-grade community halls host some of the GLMZ's most vibrant cultural gatherings, invisible to anyone who doesn't know the tunnels.

Physical culture remains a community pillar. Rugby — the sport that unified the Pacific Islands before the drownings — is played in every the Gray Zone gymnasium and Underworld open space large enough to accommodate it. Samoan martial arts and Tongan combat wrestling maintain active training halls. The physicality is not performative. It is a cultural assertion: we are here, we are strong, our bodies remember what the ocean tried to erase.

## Two Hundred Years of Intermarriage

At 2% of GLMZ genetic heritage, Pacific Islander ancestry threads through the megacity's population far beyond the visible community centers. The Ubiquitous Diaspora has done its work — names like Lautoa, Tui, Ranginui, and Faletolu appear hyphenated with every other lineage in the GLMZ. A the Gray Zone mechanic named Kovacs-Tui may never have attended a Conservancy gathering, but the name persists, carrying a fragment of Tonga through a Hungarian-Tongan marriage three generations back.

The community's small source population — 12 million across all Pacific Island nations, compared to billions in Asia or Africa — means that Pacific Islander genetic markers are dilute but widespread. Geneticists at the GLMZ Institute for Urban Demographics estimate that approximately 340,000 GLMZ residents carry measurable Pacific Islander ancestry, but fewer than 40,000 actively identify with the community. The gap between genetic heritage and cultural identity is wider for Pacific Islanders than for almost any other group, a consequence of small initial numbers dispersed across a vast population.

But those 40,000 who do identify are ferocious about it. They carry the memory of drowned nations. They maintain languages that should have died. They play rugby in tunnels under a city built a thousand miles from the nearest ocean. They are 2% of the GLMZ's genetics and 100% certain that what the water took, the people kept.
